sections.label: Listening 2

items.stem: The project started in October.
Only experienced adults were allowed to join a mobile library.
The group received help from the village librarian.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly forty people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Maha about a mobile library. When did the project begin?
Maha: It began in October, when people in a mountain village asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Maha: We started with arranging books by topic. We were supported by the village librarian, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Maha: Not really. At one point, rain damaged some book covers. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on using waterproof boxes. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Maha: I was happy when more families borrowed books. Nearly forty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Maha: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Maha: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

sections.label: Reading 2
sections.passage:
When Maha heard about a mobile library in a mountain village, the idea sounded interesting but difficult. The project had started in October, and nobody was sure how many students would join. Maha decided to attend the first meeting anyway. At the beginning, the organisers explained why the project mattered to local people. They asked everyone to listen carefully before suggesting changes.

The group began by arranging books by topic. Maha was worried about making mistakes, but the village librarian explained that learning through practice was an important part of the experience. After a few days, everyone had a specific responsibility. Some students recorded information, while others spoke to families who visited the area.

A difficulty appeared when rain damaged some book covers. The group could have stopped, but the students discussed several possibilities and chose a practical solution: using waterproof boxes. They tested the idea, checked the results and made small changes where necessary. Instead of blaming anyone for the delay, they shared the work fairly.

At the end of the month, more families borrowed books. Maha felt proud and realised that a useful project does not need to be perfect on the first day. The students presented their work to the school council and suggested that another class could continue it next term. Maha kept a notebook with photographs and reflections, hoping it would encourage younger pupils to try something similar.

Only experienced adults were allowed to join a vegetable garden.
The group received help from his science teacher.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Salim about a vegetable garden. When did the project begin?
Salim: It began in September, when people in the school courtyard asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Salim: We started with planting seeds and checking soil. We were supported by his science teacher, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Salim: Not really. At one point, the ground dried very quickly. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on collecting rainwater in tanks. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Salim: I was happy when the first vegetables were shared. Nearly thirty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Salim: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Salim: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Alya about a small local museum. When did the project begin?
Alya: It began in November, when people in an old neighbourhood asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Alya: We started with recording stories from older residents. We were supported by her grandfather, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Alya: Not really. At one point, several labels were hard to read. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on writing new labels in two languages. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Alya: I was happy when visitors understood more exhibits. Nearly fifty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Alya: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Alya: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

When Rashid heard about a safer walking route in his coastal town, the idea sounded interesting but difficult. The project had started in January, and nobody was sure how many students would join. Rashid decided to attend the first meeting anyway. At the beginning, the organisers explained why the project mattered to local people. They asked everyone to listen carefully before suggesting changes.

After a few days, everyone had a specific responsibility. Some students recorded information, while others spoke to families who visited the area.

A difficulty appeared when cars moved too fast near the gate. The group could have stopped, but the students discussed several possibilities and chose a practical solution: adding signs and a marked crossing. They tested the idea, checked the results and made small changes where necessary. Instead of blaming anyone for the delay, they shared the work fairly.

The students presented their work to the school council and suggested that another class could continue it next term. Rashid kept a notebook with photographs and reflections, hoping it would encourage younger pupils to try something similar.

sections.label: Listening 1

items.stem: What wildlife did the students record?
items.script: During the nature walk, our class observed several creatures without touching them. We saw fish beneath a bridge and read a sign about turtles. The animal we counted for our project was a small migratory bird resting near the water.

items.stem: Which device helped make the presentation?
items.script: Our digital presentation included recorded interviews with older residents. A camera provided useful photographs, and a tablet helped us organise the slides. Unfortunately, the voices were difficult to hear until a teacher lent us a better microphone for the final recording.

items.stem: Which building is the club visiting?
items.script: Our volunteering club planned to visit the history museum, but it was closed on the chosen date. We also considered holding an event at school. In the end, the members agreed to visit the hospital and deliver books to its children’s waiting area.

items.stem: What should the group carry?
items.script: The weather report says there may be showers during our fieldwork. I already have a water bottle, and my friend has packed a hat to protect her from the sun. Our teacher advised each student to bring an umbrella in case the rain begins suddenly.

items.stem: What did the children build?
items.script: In our engineering challenge, the teacher asked each team to build a structure from paper and glue. Some groups made boats, while others designed small aircraft. Our team built a bridge and tested how much weight it could carry before the paper bent.

sections.label: Listening 2

items.stem: The project started in February.
Only experienced adults were allowed to join a digital walking map.
The group received help from a history teacher.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly seventy people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Nasser about a digital walking map. When did the project begin?
Nasser: It began in February, when people in an old market asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Nasser: We started with checking routes and collecting local stories. We were supported by a history teacher, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Nasser: Not really. At one point, some street names were missing. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on asking shop owners to confirm names. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Nasser: I was happy when visitors could find landmarks easily. Nearly seventy people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Nasser: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Nasser: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

sections.label: Reading 1
texts: The first meeting for a digital walking map took place in an old market. Nasser came early to discover what volunteers would do.
Our group brought simple supplies for checking routes and collecting local stories. Nobody wanted to waste materials or spend money before planning the activity properly.
A local visitor asked why students had chosen a digital walking map. We explained how the idea could make a difference to people nearby.
During the second week, a problem appeared: some street names were missing. Some students felt worried that the whole activity might have to stop.
On the final day, Nasser presented the group’s results. Teachers and families listened carefully and asked what the students had learned.
continuations: After listening to suggestions, the team tried asking shop owners to confirm names. The new approach allowed the students to continue with their plans.
We checked everything first and worked in teams. This saved time and made the practical work much easier for the younger students.
The local aquarium displayed rare fish from deep water, and visitors learnt about underwater photography during the guided tour.
The organisers explained the main goal and gave everyone a small job. Nasser decided to help again the following week.
Everyone was pleased to hear that visitors could find landmarks easily. The group promised to share its ideas with other schools soon.
The visitor understood our explanation and asked how other classes could take part. We invited them to the next meeting.

sections.label: Reading 2
sections.passage:
When Nasser heard about a digital walking map in an old market, the idea sounded interesting but difficult. The project had started in February, and nobody was sure how many students would join. Nasser decided to attend the first meeting anyway. At the beginning, the organisers explained why the project mattered to local people. They asked everyone to listen carefully before suggesting changes.

The group began by checking routes and collecting local stories. Nasser was worried about making mistakes, but a history teacher explained that learning through practice was an important part of the experience. After a few days, everyone had a specific responsibility. Some students recorded information, while others spoke to families who visited the area.

A difficulty appeared when some street names were missing. The group could have stopped, but the students discussed several possibilities and chose a practical solution: asking shop owners to confirm names. They tested the idea, checked the results and made small changes where necessary. Instead of blaming anyone for the delay, they shared the work fairly.

At the end of the month, visitors could find landmarks easily. Nasser felt satisfied and realised that a useful project does not need to be perfect on the first day. The students presented their work to the school council and suggested that another class could continue it next term. Nasser kept a notebook with photographs and reflections, hoping it would encourage younger pupils to try something similar.
